analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and replaces it with tax credits, high-risk pools, and looser insurance rules.
analysis.headline: The repeal bill, referred to ten House committees, never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the Affordable Care Act outright, erasing it as if it had never been enacted, and replaced it with a smaller package: tax credits for people buying private insurance, state high-risk pools for people with pre-existing conditions, association health plans and "individual membership associations" for buying coverage outside many state rules, and national caps on malpractice damages [S2, S3]. It was referred to ten House committees, sent to two subcommittees, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended [S1, S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill had passed, health insurers would have gained the most: association health plans and "individual membership associations" would have been exempted from many state benefit mandates, and insurers could have sold individual coverage across state lines under the rules of one chosen state [S2, S3]. Physicians and their insurers would have gained national caps on malpractice damages and a new bad-debt tax deduction for charity care [S2, S3]. Small employers would have gotten a tax credit for setting up auto-enrollment [S3]. Uninsured low-income people would have received a refundable tax credit for private insurance, but only if their state ran a high-risk pool, and the credit phases out quickly with income [S2, S3].

how_it_helps.text: Uninsured low-income people would have received a refundable tax credit for private health insurance, worth up to $2,000 per individual ($4,000 per couple) plus $500 per dependent, phasing out one percentage point for every $1,000 of income above 200% of the poverty line

The bill would have created association health plans letting small businesses and trade associations pool together to buy coverage, and individual membership associations doing the same for individuals
States would have received $300 million a year in block grants for high-risk pools covering people who cannot get affordable coverage because of a medical condition
The bill would have required state CHIP programs to specify how they will cover 90% of targeted low-income children
Doctors would have gained a tax deduction for bad debt from emergency care they are required to provide without payment

analysis.who_pays: If the bill had passed, the people who bore the cost would have been those with pre-existing conditions (who would have lost the law's guarantee that insurers must sell them coverage and must price it without regard to health), low- and moderate-income people (whose ACA premium subsidies and planned Medicaid expansion would have disappeared in favor of a smaller, faster-phasing-out tax credit), patients injured by medical malpractice (whose damages would have been capped), some children above 300% of the poverty line (who would have become ineligible for CHIP), and state budgets (which would have lost federal stimulus assistance and seen Medicaid hospital payments cut) [S2, S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: People with pre-existing conditions and state budgets

drawbacks.text: Repealing the ACA would have removed its guarantee that insurers must sell coverage to people with pre-existing conditions and cannot charge them more for it; the bill's replacement, state high-risk pools, is optional for states and funded at only $300 million a year nationally

The low-income tax credit phases out one percentage point per $1,000 of income above 200% of the poverty line, so help disappears quickly and there is no guarantee any affordable plan exists to buy with it

National caps on malpractice damages and shortened filing windows reduce compensation for patients injured by medical negligence, the strongest good-faith objection supporters of the liability limits must answer

The bill cuts Medicaid and CHIP: it bars CHIP payments for children in families above 300% of the poverty line and reduces Medicaid DSH hospital payments, while rescinding state fiscal assistance from the 2009 stimulus law

The bill's declared offsets are unspecified 'savings from health care efficiencies,' rescissions of stimulus money, and spending caps, with no independent estimate that they cover the cost of the new tax credits

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill did contain real help: tax credits for low-income uninsured people, high-risk pool grants, association plans for small businesses, and a requirement that CHIP programs plan to cover 90% of targeted low-income children. But the deal's core was repeal of a law that had just extended guaranteed coverage to millions, and the replacement was thinner: the tax credit phases out fast, the high-risk pools depend on state action and a small annual appropriation, and association plans work partly by escaping state benefit mandates. People with pre-existing conditions, Medicaid-eligible adults, malpractice plaintiffs, and state budgets would have absorbed the losses. The replacement did not match what it repealed.

outcome.mechanism: It got sent to ten committees and then to two subcommittees, sat there with no hearing or vote, and quietly expired when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Wilson introduced the bill on March 25, 2010, one week after President Obama signed the Affordable Care Act into law, and it was referred to ten House committees the same day
In April 2010 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee and the Education and Labor Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions
No hearing, markup, or vote on the bill is recorded after the subcommittee referrals
The bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, without either chamber ever voting on it

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who would have lost coverage or protections under the bill came out ahead: the Affordable Care Act's guarantees for people with pre-existing conditions, its premium subsidies, and its Medicaid expansion all remained in force because the repeal never advanced. The insurer and provider provisions it contained died with it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who kept Affordable Care Act protections

for.name: Rep. Joe Wilson
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, which would have repealed the Affordable Care Act and replaced it with tax credits, association health plans, and malpractice caps

against.name: Rep. Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Presided over a House that referred the bill to ten committees and never brought it to the floor; the bill received no further action after subcommittee referral

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held primary jurisdiction over the bill's core insurance provisions but never reported it out; it was referred to the Health Subcommittee in April 2010 and no vote was ever scheduled

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the Democratic-controlled House took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill's centerpiece for this industry is regulatory relief: association health plans and IMAs escape many state benefit mandates, and individual policies can be sold nationwide under one issuer-chosen state's rules. These mechanisms let insurers sell skimpier coverage to healthier customers, which raises prices for everyone left in the fully regulated pool.

The bill caps malpractice damages nationally, limits the time to sue, and gives doctors a bad-debt deduction for charity care. Supporters argue this lowers malpractice insurance costs; injured patients bear the reduced compensation.
National caps on noneconomic and punitive damages and shortened filing windows directly reduce recoveries in malpractice cases, opposing the interests of injured patients the bar represents.

Small employers would get a tax credit for adopting auto-enrollment and access to association health plans, but the bill also requires employers to disclose what they spend on health coverage on workers' tax forms.
